subject: maths
title: Percentages: out of a hundred
intro: Percentages are everywhere — sale prices, test scores, phone batteries, statistics in the news. The good news is that a percentage is just a fraction with a fixed bottom number: 100. Once you see 'per cent' as 'per hundred', finding percentages, discounts and increases becomes straightforward arithmetic you can do in your head or on paper.

sections.heading: Per cent means per hundred
body: The word **per cent** literally means 'per hundred'. So **45%** means 45 out of every 100, which is the fraction **45/100** and the decimal **0.45**. These three — percentage, fraction, decimal — are just different outfits for the same number.

To turn a percentage into a decimal, divide by 100 (move the point two places left): 45% becomes 0.45. To go back, multiply by 100: 0.7 becomes 70%. Being able to switch between them quickly is half the skill.

diagram.caption: 45% means 45 squares out of a hundred are shaded.

sections.heading: Finding a percentage of an amount
body: To find a percentage **of** a number, turn the percentage into a decimal and multiply. '25% of 80' becomes 0.25 × 80. Some percentages have handy shortcuts: **10%** is just divide by 10, **50%** is half, **25%** is a quarter, and **1%** is divide by 100. You can build others from these — 30% is three lots of 10%.
This is exactly what you're doing when you work out a tip, a tax, or how many questions you got right on a test.

steps: 5% is half of 10%, so 5% of 60 is 3.

sections.heading: Discounts and increases
body: A **discount** takes a percentage off. A quick way: if something is 25% off, you **pay 75%** of the price (because 100% − 25% = 75%). So multiply the price by 0.75. Working with what you *keep* is faster than finding the discount and subtracting.
An **increase** works the same way in reverse. A 20% increase means you end with 120% of the original, so multiply by 1.2. This 'multiplier' trick handles tax, interest and price rises in one step.

example.problem: A jacket costs $40 and is reduced by 30%. What is the sale price?
steps: A 30% discount means you pay 100% − 30% = 70% of the price.

sections.heading: A common trap
body: Percentages of *different* amounts don't cancel out. If a price goes **up 10%** and then **down 10%**, you do **not** get back to where you started — the second 10% is taken from a bigger number, so you end up slightly lower. Always ask 'a percentage of what?' before combining them.
Whenever a question mixes two percentage changes, work them out one step at a time on the actual amounts, rather than adding or subtracting the percentages.

practice.q: What is 60% written as a decimal?
practice.explain: Per cent means per hundred, so divide by 100: 60 ÷ 100 = 0.6.

practice.q: A $50 item is 20% off. What do you pay?

practice.explain: 75% is three quarters; a quarter of 40 is 10, so three quarters is 30. (Or 0.75 × 40 = 30.)

practice.q: A price rises 10%, then falls 10%. Compared with the start, the final price is:
practice.explain: The second 10% is taken from a larger amount than the first was added to, so you end up slightly below the original price.

summary: Per cent means per hundred: 45% = 45/100 = 0.45 — the same number three ways.
To find a percentage of an amount, turn it into a decimal and multiply; use 10%, 50%, 25% and 1% as shortcuts.
For a discount, multiply by what you keep (25% off → ×0.75); for an increase, multiply by more than 1 (20% up → ×1.2).
Percentage changes of different amounts don't cancel — always ask 'a percentage of what?'
